commenti.body:
I watched this film recently and wrote a [review on Letterboxd](https://boxd.it/6yjI6z).

Here is a small part of the review about my opinion on the ending:

*I would usually say it was the Doctor's skill that saved her, but we just saw the little girl ask Johannes to save Inger's life. This way, Dreyer lets the viewer decide for their own in what they want to believe—even though some viewers aren't religious, he still wants to bring forward the idea that miracles do exist. Maybe he wants us to be more like the little girl?*

Yeah, I think there's definitely a call to rediscover the inner child that gets lost when one becomes a rational adult and loses that childhood wonder/naivety. I would say I agree with yourmostly about the ambiguous stance on the correct world view, but I do feel that Dreyer is very much confirming that miracles do exist with that ending and is somewhat rejecting the rational, scientific view of the world. I'll definitely need to rewatch it to clarify my thoughts.
In the eternal words of George Michael: Cause I gotta have faith.

The play (and movie) deals with the struggle between faith and reason and I think it's pretty clearly on the side of faith. The movie may be more ambiguous, but the play is pretty clearly saying that salvation comes only through the unwavering irrational faith of a child, that any attempt to rationalize the faith and reconcile faith with reason is wrong. It's an awful play, and Kaj Munk who wrote it had nazi sympathies before he turned on them (and they turned on him).
Makes sense, especially with the reference to Kierkegaard and his notion of "a leap of faith."

For the record Dreyer shot two versions of the ending. One version made the ending more ambiguous about whether she was really brought back to life, and the other ending  was a genuine miracle. Dreyer went with the genuine miracle ending. So it was intentional on his part to show something that really happened.

While you're absolutely right that Munk admired both Hitler and Mussolini in the early 1930's and wrote positively about their "strong man" leadership (being against democracy himself), I feel it needs saying that Munk's turning against them in the late 1930's (before the war) was very vocal, including writing several plays that overtly criticised Nazi Germany, and during the occupation of Denmark, he was a leading figure in the resistance. Ultimately executed by the Nazis, he is celebrated to this day for his unapologetic resistance.


There is nothing wrong at all with your comment, I just wanted to expand to which degree he turned on Nazism, and that his legacy is that of a fierce opponent of all things Nazi.
Ordet's ending is definitely something that sparks varied interpretations. Your reading of it is quite insightful. Maybe Dreyer was playing on multiple levels at once? Quite the discussion starter.

I don't think it's metaphorical or allegorical at all. She literally does wake up. We see it with our own eyes and there is nothing at all to suggest we're not meant to believe that that is literally happening. 

The question is of course - why? And there's no really good answer for it. It seems phenomenally unlikely that a person could be "dead" for so long as to go on and carry out a funeral for them, only for them to "return" to life during the funeral. And yet, it does happen.

I don't think we're meant to solve this like it's a puzzle or something. I think the question and its seeming unanswerableness is the exact point. I'm only half joking when I say, basically, this falls under what I broadly categorize as "movie magic." Not in the sense of depicting literal magic, but rather depicting something that would be essentially impossible in real life, actually almost ridiculous to the point of absurdity, but doing it with an absolute mastery of technique and craft and total sincerity, and forcing the viewer to accept it as reality. That is, in my view, literally all that we're supposed to take from it. I don't believe we're meant to debate over whether the film is or isn't depicting reality - it is. If Dreyer wants us to debate anything, it's \*why\* that seemingly impossible thing happened.
That's fascinating considering the rest of his filmography, which seems to lean quite heavily into criticizing religion.

I don’t think you have to read it as an endorsement of religion and religious miracles, as you say Dreyer’s work isn’t typically pro-religion and I believe he’s refuted the idea it’s pro-religion. 

I read it as a comment on how rigid our belief systems are, and how things can be hard to accept when you limit yourselves so much. It’s about being open and accepting of difference and not shutting down things you don’t understand.
He criticizes organised religion sure, but not belief in God. He was religious himself.

I believe resurrection does take place in order to prove that our weirdest dreams can be unfolding in front of us and we might be rejecting them for the sake of reason. An invitation to embrace the diversity of life beyond our comprehension.
